LESSON 5 OF 106·Cyber Security Fundamentals

Attack Surface & Attack Vectors

Attack surface and attack vector are different things: one is how many doors you have, the other is the path an attacker actually walks. Learn to reduce both.

Beginner13 min
Why this matters

Attack surface is everything an attacker can reach. Attack vectors are the specific routes they use. Reducing surface is one of the most reliable ways to reduce risk.

  1. Vector: An attacker or faulty client alters parameters, headers, timing, or sequence order.

  1. Verification: Remove anything you do not need; the cheapest control is the service you never deployed.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Surface includes network-exposed ports, public web endpoints, mobile application code, third-party scripts, and user-facing input.
  • A vector is a concrete path, such as credential reuse, an unpatched dependency, a malicious attachment, or a misconfigured storage bucket.
  • Attackers enumerate surface automatically and continuously, so anything reachable is discovered eventually.
  • Reducing surface means removing reachability, not merely hiding it, because hidden interfaces are still exploitable.
  • Each exposed service is also an operational and patching commitment you must keep.

The background

  • The term comes from physical security, where an attack surface is the exposed exterior of a defended building.
  • Software engineering adopted it in the 1990s as internet-facing services multiplied.
  • Cloud computing widened surface again, because storage, queues and serverless functions become reachable through credentials rather than ports.
  • Modern frameworks add supply-chain surface, because one compromised dependency reaches every consumer at once.

Real-world examples

  • An object-storage bucket left publicly readable is a single misconfiguration that exposes far more data than the application ever did.
  • A forgotten admin endpoint still running in production is common surface that nobody is testing any more.
  • A third-party analytics script on a payment page inherits the trust of the page it is embedded in.

What to look for

  • List every externally reachable host, port, hostname and API endpoint, including test environments.
  • Check for default credentials, sample applications and debug modes left enabled.
  • Look for internal services that assume the network is trusted.
  • Review third-party and supply-chain dependencies, not only your own code.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Remove anything you do not need; the cheapest control is the service you never deployed.
  • Restrict reachability with network policy, private subnets and identity-based access.
  • Run internet-wide discovery continuously and alert on new exposure.
  • Patch and maintain every service you choose to keep reachable.
